The Greek company PPC, the leading South-East European integrated utility Group, will acquire the two companies, including all 38 ABO Energy employees in the two countries, a development pipeline with a total capacity of around two gigawatts, and five operational solar parks with a combined capacity of 82 megawatts as well as a 17 megawatts solar farm nearing completion. The sale will have no impact on the development of ABO Energy’s planned restructuring and financing solution. 'Following the sale of our Greek subsidiary and most of our Finnish wind power pipeline, the sale of our Hungarian and Polish subsidiaries marks another step towards focusing on those countries where we can achieve sustainable long-term commercial success,' said Managing Director Dr Karsten Schlageter . 'We are pleased to have found a good solution both for ABO Energy and for the employees concerned.' Subject to the necessary regulatory approvals, closing of the transaction is expected by the end of the year. ABO Energy has been active as a project developer in Poland and Hungary since 2019. During this time, the company has developed and sold renewable energy projects in both countries while building a substantial development pipeline. ABO Energy’s objective remains unchanged: to agree a sustainable restructuring and financing solution for the company in the coming weeks and months. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said on Tuesday that Lithuania is ready to pay the cost to set up a permanent US military base if Washington should âagree to establish one there, a day after US President Donald Trump said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent base. Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, on the same day, said that the possible deployment of a NATO military base and nuclear weapons in Lithuania would further escalate tensions. "Both of these things will not contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will become another significant round in the escalation of tensions," Peskov said. Peskov added that if such deployment occurs, Russia would be forced to take retaliatory measures to ensure its national security. A constitutional amendment to lift a ban on weapons of mass destruction, potentially opening the way for stationing NATO nuclear weapons in Lithuania, passed the first reading in the Lithuanian parliament earlier on Tuesday. A final vote on the amendment has been scheduled for January 12, 2027. Lithuania, a member of the EU and NATO, shares a border with Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad. The United States has kept an armored battalion of almost 1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning âthe troops arrive and leave every few months. Sinkevicius said he proposed turning this into a permanent presence at a meeting with Trump's envoy John Coale last month in Vilnius. The latest development comes as Russia recently issued a warning over NATO's military activities in the Baltic region, saying it is prepared to use all means at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO attempts to blockade Russia's Kaliningrad region. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte responded last week by describing NATO as a "defensive alliance" and condemning what he called Russia's "nuclear threats." Moscow said it poses no threat to anyone. The exchange has remained largely rhetorical, but highlights rising tensions around Kaliningrad and the broader Baltic region. The recent tensions in the Baltic appear to be directly linked to repeated drone disputes between Russia and Baltic coastal states, while NATO has increasingly pressured Russia by targeting its socioeconomic stability, said Chen Yu, deputy director of the Institute of Eurasian Studies at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations. More fundamentally, Chen said, this is the inevitable result of a shift in NATO's Baltic strategy: after the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict since February 2022, NATO's presence in the Baltic has gradually upgraded from rotational deterrence to permanent basing, pushing military pressure right up to Russia's border. Chen said the Baltic states hope to use nuclear deterrence to offset Russia's military power, driven by rising security anxiety and a desire to align with US strategic agenda, as Washington actively discusses expanding its nuclear deployment plans in Europe. In response, he said, Russia is likely to further strengthen its nuclear forces in Kaliningrad, deploy more tactical nuclear weapons and hypersonic weapons, and enhance the nuclear-conventional strike capability of its Baltic Fleet so as to defend its red lines while avoiding being cornered into a full confrontation.
